subject: maths

moments.title: Euler in St Petersburg
moments.who: Leonhard Euler, St Petersburg Academy of Sciences
moments.body:
Leonhard Euler, born in Basel and a student of Johann Bernoulli, arrives in St Petersburg in 1727 at age 20. He works at the new Imperial Academy under Empress Catherine I's patronage.

He produces foundational work in mechanics, fluid dynamics, music theory, and pure mathematics. He loses sight in his right eye in 1735 (from a fever, or perhaps overwork).
moments.takeaway: Euler begins a career that will produce more mathematics than any one human had before or since.

moments.title: Solving the Königsberg bridges and the Basel problem
moments.body:
Euler solves the Königsberg bridges problem — the start of graph theory and topology.

In the same year, he solves the Basel problem: sum of 1/n^2 for n from 1 to infinity equals pi^2/6. This problem had defeated Leibniz, Jakob and Johann Bernoulli, and many others. Euler's solution links analysis, number theory, and the constant pi in a deep, surprising way.

quote.text: If you cannot solve a problem, then there is an easier problem you can solve: find it.
quote.attrib: Attributed to George Polya, in the spirit of Euler

moments.takeaway: Euler proves the sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... equals pi^2/6 — connecting pi to integers in a deeply unexpected way.

moments.title: Euler in Berlin
moments.body:
Frederick the Great hires Euler for the Berlin Academy. Euler spends 25 years producing prolifically: 'Introductio in analysin infinitorum' (1748), 'Institutiones calculi differentialis' (1755), foundational work in number theory, mechanics, optics, astronomy.

He writes letters to Princess Anhalt-Dessau on physics and philosophy, which are published as 'Letters to a German Princess' — one of the most popular science books of the 18th century.

The identity e^(i pi) + 1 = 0 — connecting five fundamental constants — is a special case of his formula e^(i x) = cos x + i sin x (1748).
moments.takeaway: Euler's identity has been called the most beautiful equation in mathematics. It is one line in a vast body of work.

moments.title: Euler returns to St Petersburg, goes blind
moments.body:
Catherine the Great recalls Euler. Within a year of his return, a cataract takes his remaining sight. Now totally blind, Euler dictates papers to assistants and his sons.

The rate of his output actually INCREASES. He computes mentally and dictates; his sons write down the results. About half of his 800+ papers were produced in this final blind period.

He dies of a brain hemorrhage on 18 September 1783, while playing with his grandchildren. His last words, calculating Uranus's orbit: 'I die.'
moments.takeaway: Blindness doesn't slow Euler. He keeps producing groundbreaking mathematics for 17 more years.

moments.title: Euler's collected works begin publication
moments.body:
Beginning in 1907 (Euler's bicentenary), the Swiss Academy of Sciences begins publishing Euler's complete works (Opera Omnia). The project is STILL not complete — over 80 volumes have appeared and more are planned.

Euler published about 850 papers and books, and left behind thousands of letters. He's estimated to be responsible for about 30% of all mathematical, physical and mechanical research of the 18th century.
moments.takeaway: Euler's output is so vast that publishing his works has taken over 115 years and counting.

now.title: Euler's legacy today
now.body:
Euler's name is attached to more theorems, equations, formulas, and constants than any other mathematician. e (Euler's number), Euler's formula, Euler's identity, the Euler-Lagrange equations, the Euler characteristic, the totient function, the Euler product, Eulerian paths, Euler diagrams, Euler angles, Euler-Mascheroni constant.

His work is foundational to mathematical analysis, number theory, mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, music theory, and graph theory.
now.open_questions: What remains in unpublished Euler manuscripts? How much of modern mathematics could be reconstructed from Euler alone if everything else were lost? Why was one person so productive?

reflection: Euler's productivity is almost incomprehensible. Even modern mathematicians, supported by computers and large research groups, rarely produce one-tenth as much. Some of his peers — Lagrange, Laplace — were also astonishingly productive. How do we explain this concentration? Was it the specific conditions of 18th-century mathematics (much low-hanging fruit), or were these individuals just exceptionally gifted?
